hints: Compare the oxidation numbers in the table for Br in $\text{Br}_{2}$ and Br in $\text{HBr}$, and for C in $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$ and C in $\text{CO}_{2}$, to see which element is reduced.
walkthrough:
Link oxidising agent to reduction**
Think of an oxidising agent as an electron acceptor. It takes electrons from the other reactant, so it itself gets reduced. In oxidation number terms, reduction always means a decrease in oxidation number.

Apply the table values**
Look at bromine: Br in $\text{Br}_{2}$ is 0 and Br in $\text{HBr}$ is -1. That is a decrease, so bromine is reduced. At the same time C goes from +2 in $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$ to +4 in $\text{CO}_{2}$, an increase, so methanoic acid is oxidised. The species that is reduced is the oxidising agent.
Final answer: $\text{Br}_{2}$ / bromine is the oxidising agent as the oxidation number of Br decreases from 0 to -1.

hints: Recall the characteristic colour of aqueous $\text{Br}_{2}$ and think what happens to that colour as $\text{Br}_{2}$ is used up to form colourless $\text{HBr}$.
walkthrough:
Picture the reactants and products**
Aqueous bromine is a familiar coloured reagent. It is brown or orange. The products are $\text{HBr(aq)}$, which is colourless in solution, and $\text{CO}_{2}(\text{g})$, which escapes as bubbles.

Pick the clear visual change**
As $\text{Br}_{2}$ is consumed, its brown or orange colour fades. So you see decolourisation to a colourless solution. Effervescence from $\text{CO}_{2}$ is also happening, but the colour change is the classic test for loss of bromine.
Final answer: The brown / orange / red solution turns colourless / decolourises.

hints: Read the initial $[\text{Br}_{2}]$ at 0 s and the final $[\text{Br}_{2}]$ at 600 s from the graph, remembering the axis is $[\text{Br}_{2}] \times 10^{5}$.
Recall that average rate = change in concentration divided by time taken, and think what units concentration divided by time gives.
walkthrough:
Read the two concentrations**
At time 0 s the graph starts at $100 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. At 600 s it has levelled to about $12 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. So the total fall is $(100 - 12) \times 10^{-5} = 88 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Divide by the time interval**
Average rate is simply change over time:
$$\text{rate} = \frac{\Delta[\text{Br}_{2}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{88 \times 10^{-5}}{600}$$
That gives $1.47 \times 10^{-6}$. Units come from concentration divided by time, so $\text{mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

Final answer: change in $[\text{Br}_{2}] = (100 - 12) \times 10^{-5} = 88 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$$\text{average rate} = \frac{88 \times 10^{-5}}{600} = 1.47 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

hints: Think how a faster reaction at higher temperature affects the steepness at the start, while the starting amount of $\text{Br}_{2}$ and the overall stoichiometry stay the same.
walkthrough:
Sketch the faster curve**
Higher temperature means faster reaction, so at every early time more $\text{Br}_{2}$ has been used up. Start at the same point on the y axis, but draw the line dropping more steeply at the beginning and staying below the original curve.

Keep the end point the same**
You start with the same initial concentrations, so the same amount of $\text{Br}_{2}$ is eventually consumed. The new curve must flatten to the same final $[\text{Br}_{2}]$ value, just reaching it sooner.
Final answer: Curve with steeper initial gradient than the $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ curve, falling more quickly but levelling off at the same final $[\text{Br}_{2}]$.

hints: Consider what happens to the average kinetic energy of the reactant particles when temperature is raised.
Link this energy change to the activation energy barrier and the proportion of collisions that can lead to reaction.
walkthrough:
See what heating does to energy**
Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy. Warm the mixture from $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ and every particle on average moves faster and carries more kinetic energy.

Connect energy to successful collisions**
For reaction, colliding particles must have combined energy at least equal to the activation energy, $E_{a}$. With higher average energy, many more particles exceed $E_{a}$. Collision frequency rises only slightly, but the proportion of collisions that are successful rises sharply, so overall rate rises sharply.

Final answer: At higher temperature the average kinetic energy of particles increases.
A greater proportion of particles / collisions have energy greater than or equal to $E_{a}$, so frequency of successful collisions increases.

hints: Count the bonds in $\text{H-C(=O)-O-H}$: three single bonds plus one double bond, and remember each shared pair is shown as one dot plus one cross in the overlap.
Give each oxygen a full octet by adding lone pairs: each O already has two shared pairs in bonds, so work out how many non bonding pairs are needed to reach eight outer electrons.
walkthrough:
Place the shared pairs**
Draw $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$ as $\text{H-C(=O)-O-H}$. In each overlap put the bonding electrons: one dot and one cross for each single bond ($\text{H-C}$, $\text{C-O}$, $\text{O-H}$) and two dots plus two crosses for the $\text{C=O}$ double bond. Show outer electrons only.

Complete the octets with lone pairs**
Carbon already has four shared pairs, so it has a full shell with no lone pairs. Each oxygen has only two shared pairs so far. Add two lone pairs (four dots or crosses) on the $\text{C=O}$ oxygen and two lone pairs on the $\text{O-H}$ oxygen, giving each oxygen eight outer electrons in total.

Final answer: H-C single bond (1 dot + 1 cross), C=O double bond (2 dots + 2 crosses), C-O single bond (1 dot + 1 cross), O-H single bond (1 dot + 1 cross).
Each O has 2 lone pairs (4 non bonding electrons) to complete octet; C and H have no lone pairs.
